hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the 64 binary agreement counters with an equivalent direction
and confidence representation. Keep 64 agreement-direction bits D in
individually updated flip-flops, reset to one. Store 64 strong/weak bits
S in a native 64x1 distributed RAM: S=1 is strong and S=0 is weak.
For original binary state C, D=C[1] and S=(C[1]==C[0]); conversely
C={D, S ? D : !D}. All four saturating-counter states remain represented.

For an accepted training event with agreement outcome A, read the current
D and S at the event's index and implement exactly:
    next_D = S ? D : A
    next_S = (D == A)
Both expressions use the OLD state. Update the indexed direction flop
only when S is weak; strong events leave it unchanged. Write next_S
through the RAM's single synchronous write port. No incrementer,
decrementer, saturation comparators or second confidence read is needed.
Keep the fetch lookup exactly agreements[PC[7:2]] from the direction
flops; neither RAM data nor a confidence-valid mux enters this path.
Retain all 64 entries and the original unfurled PC index.

Register each qualified EX branch event as valid, six-bit index and
agreement. The next cycle reads current direction and confidence at
that registered index and updates both stores on its ending edge.
Clear event validity when no new event arrives. Accept and consume one
event per cycle, including consecutive writes to the same index, without
reading a saved fetch-time counter or stale training snapshot. The
confidence RAM has one asynchronous training read and one synchronous
write; the direction vector has independent fetch and training lookups.
A pending event completes during frontend/data stalls, divider holds
or a younger recovery. Preserve existing EX training qualification.

Use an explicit distributed_ram attribute and no array reset for S.
Reset D to all ones, start a six-bit scrub address at zero, assert
initialization, and cancel pending training. Write S=0 at indices 0
through 63 on the first 64 non-reset edges, independently of pipeline
stalls. Discard new events and suppress direction updates during scrub.
Fetch naturally uses D=1 as static backward-taken/forward-not-taken
prediction during this interval, with direct aligned JAL prediction
still active. Clear initialization after the index-63 write; accept
the first dynamic event on the following edge. Reset at any point
restarts the scrub and resets directions. Uninitialized confidence
must never enable a direction update or affect fetch.

At a lookup/update crossing, the accepted instruction uses the pre-edge
direction and carries that predicted_taken bit through ID/EX. Delayed
training may change predictions relative to immediate baseline updates,
but existing EX recovery remains authoritative. Do not add an event
bypass to fetch or register the confidence read across another cycle.
Verify RAM inference; replacing the confidence array with 64 resettable
flops would not establish the intended storage architecture.

Preserve the single PC register, exact legal/aligned B/J targets,
unconditional aligned JAL prediction, unpredicted JALR, same-cycle EX
recovery, validity-only squashes, raw source-index paths, payload holds,
forwarding and the nine-cycle divider schedule. Keep nret=1, all RVFI
fields, order, legality, traps, memory handshakes and bounded progress
unchanged. No fetch queue, PC-bank change, return stack, global history,
new execution stage or arithmetic-unit optimization is proposed.

The expected benefit is compact hysteresis storage and a small shared
training datapath without paying native RAM latency on fetch prediction.
The registered event also keeps late EX resolution out of the confidence
read/write recurrence. Principal risks are the training direction-read
mux, weak-state write-enable fanout and an unchanged ALU/divider timing
bottleneck. Forecast confidence is low; measure the actual circuit.

Validate against an independent ordinary two-bit binary-counter oracle,
not equations copied from the new encoding. Cover all eight state/event
transitions, saturation, consecutive same-index events, read/update
collisions, initialization boundaries, reset in every scrub phase and
while an event is pending, and arbitrary stalls/divider holds. Use long
tests beyond 64 cycles because the unchanged short formal window covers
startup fallback rather than dynamic confidence updates. Preserve all
architectural, exact-once and ten-cycle progress assertions. Run the
unchanged formal suite, full RVFI cosim and canonical stalled CoreMark
with every CRC, UART validation, bounds, completion and timing marker.
Evaluate median Gowin Fmax across all three placement options and verify
native confidence RAM inference. Accept only if fitness exceeds
182.46424 iterations/second; unchanged 4,230,003 cycles would require
more than 77.18243 MHz.

An isolated prototype of this exact split-state design passed a
6,000-cycle independent binary-counter oracle, including repeated
reset, initialization, all four counter states and consecutive aliases.
Canonical stalled CoreMark retained 4,230,003 bracketed cycles and passed
all CRCs, UART validation, bounds, completion and marker checks. Vendor
placement options 0/1/2 measured 67.929, 68.089 and 68.089 MHz, median
68.089 MHz, with 5,308 LUT4s, 1,165 registers and 44 LUT RAMs in option
zero. The four added LUT RAMs confirm native confidence storage. The
worst reported path was the unchanged first divider recurrence.
This yields approximately 160.967 iterations/second, a 7.72 percent
regression from 174.44, so the proposed timing benefit was not observed
and the champion must remain. The forecast below records the measured
result rather than the original six-percent expectation. Full formal
and full-RVFI cosim of this exact final prototype remain implementation
gates; the independent unit test and CRC run do not replace them.

title: Reset register-file validity instead of distributed RAM contents
motivation:
The champion scores 174.44 iterations/sec at 73.790 MHz and 4,230,003
bracketed CoreMark cycles. Earlier forwarding/mux refinements r11s0 and
r12s0 did not exceed the acceptance margin, and r13s0's divisor fanout
change regressed. The register file still synchronously clears every
32-bit storage word despite its distributed-RAM attribute. Preserve
reset-visible zero values with per-register written bits so the data
RAM itself can use a simpler write port without a bulk-reset path.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion scores 174.44 iterations/sec at 73.790 MHz and 4,230,003
bracketed CoreMark cycles. Earlier forwarding/mux refinements r11s0 and
r12s0 did not exceed the acceptance margin, and r13s0's divisor fanout
change regressed. The register file still synchronously clears every
32-bit storage word despite its distributed-RAM attribute. Preserve

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the register file's synchronous bulk data reset with a 32-bit
written bitmap. Keep the same 32x32 distributed-RAM array and the exact
public clock/reset/read/write interface. This is one local storage and
reset-control micro-optimization; no pipeline or ISA change is involved.

On reset clear written_q to zero. Otherwise, a write with w_en and
w_addr!=0 sets written_q[w_addr]. Update regs[w_addr] only when !reset,
w_en and w_addr!=0. The regs array must have no reset loop or reset
assignment. Reset takes priority over both an architectural write and
setting its written bit; x0's bit is never set. Existing data may remain
physically in RAM after reset but must never become architecturally
visible until the corresponding register is written again.

For each read port retain this exact priority: return zero for x0;
otherwise return w_data on a same-cycle write-first hit; otherwise return
regs[read_addr] if written_q[read_addr] is set, and zero if it is clear.
Preserve the original combinational bypass during reset as well: reset
suppresses writes on the clock edge, but does not newly gate the existing
w_en-qualified read bypass. Both ports must independently implement the
same rules. Never clear the RAM incrementally, stall the CPU to reset it,
change instruction timing, or let unknown/unwritten storage escape.

The intended benefit is removing the bulk-clear requirement
from the distributed data array while retaining every visible reset
value. Gowin may infer fewer distributed RAM resources and a simpler
write/reset network. The cost is a small resettable bitmap and read-zero
qualification; these can instead lengthen decode, so vendor measurement
is essential. Retain the distributed-RAM inference attribute and portable
SystemVerilog; add no vendor-only primitive or synthesis-only behavior.

An isolated prototype of these exact nested read priorities passed the
existing register-file runner and both pipeline runners with unchanged
assertions. Gowin placement options 0/1/2 measured 68.250, 76.260 and
76.260 MHz, median 76.260 MHz. Option zero used 5,281 LUT4s, 1,233
registers and 32 LUT RAMs, versus the champion's 5,422, 1,214 and 40.
BSRAM and DSP counts remained four and two. At unchanged CoreMark cycles
this projects 180.2836 iter/sec, about 3.35 percent above the champion.
This is below the 4.6-percent acceptance margin, not an accepted gain.
The integer three-percent forecast reflects this preliminary measurement.
Full RVFI cosimulation subsequently passed selftest and all three random
programs, each with and without simultaneous instruction/data bus stalls
(eight passing cases). Canonical CoreMark passed all five CRCs, required
UART validation, memory bounds and timing brackets, with exactly
4,230,003 bracketed cycles. The resulting prototype fitness is 180.2836
iterations/sec. Full-core standard formal remains an implementation gate;
these simulation results must not be described as a completed formal proof.

An additional dirty-all-registers/reset/write-collision/selective-rewrite
test passed without inspecting physical RAM contents. A six-step bounded
SAT comparison against the original register file also passed: reset is
asserted at step one, both read outputs are compared at steps two through
six, and subsequent addresses, writes, data and resets are symbolic.
The candidate RAM is not initialized to zero by the proof. This bounded
register-file result does not replace the full-core formal gate.

Retain and extend existing tests to dirty every nonzero register, reset
again, then verify all 32 read as zero through both ports. Exercise reset
coincident with writes, x0 writes, repeated reset, distinct and identical
read addresses, writes immediately after reset, uninitialized registers,
and same-cycle bypass before the first stored write. Check a write to one
register cannot expose stale data in any other register. Exercise WB
write-first dependencies, held operands and both buses stalled in pipeline
tests. Prove/reset-check the architectural read behavior independently of
the physical RAM contents; do not initialize the unreset array in formal
to make the property pass.

Keep the nret=1 IO, decoder legality, RVFI operands/order, traps, original
forwarding and hold priorities, and real/ALTOPS arithmetic unchanged.
Run the unchanged standard formal and RVFI cosimulation gates and retain
all canonical CoreMark CRC/UART/bounds/marker checks. Expect exactly
4,230,003 bracketed cycles with the same stall sequence. Acceptance needs
fitness strictly above 182.46424 iter/sec, approximately 77.184 MHz at
that cycle count; retain the champion unless that margin is measured.

title: Elastic issue with operand-stage-aware hazards and late store-data forwarding
motivation:
Structural r10s1 showed that a one-entry fall-through fetch buffer
reduces CoreMark cycles from 4,230,003 to 4,022,833. Its 72.497 MHz
median and 180.21 iter/sec missed the 182.46424 acceptance threshold.
The larger queues of r11s1-r13s1 saved few additional cycles while
adding selection and operand-storage costs. The current interlock
also compares both raw instruction fields against every late producer,
even when a field is an immediate or the only dependency is store data.
Store data is consumed in MEM, one stage after its address is needed.
Exploit that distinction in a small elastic issue design, targeting
additional cycle savings without replicating register-file ports or
adding a combinational load-to-ALU bypass.

hypothesis.motivation:
Structural r10s1 showed that a one-entry fall-through fetch buffer
reduces CoreMark cycles from 4,230,003 to 4,022,833. Its 72.497 MHz
median and 180.21 iter/sec missed the 182.46424 acceptance threshold.
The larger queues of r11s1-r13s1 saved few additional cycles while
adding selection and operand-storage costs. The current interlock
also compares both raw instruction fields against every late producer,
even when a field is an immediate or the only dependency is store data.
Store data is consumed in MEM, one stage after its address is needed.
Exploit that distinction in a small elastic issue design, targeting
additional cycle savings without replicating register-file ports or
adding a combinational load-to-ALU bypass.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Build an operand-stage-aware elastic issue path: retain the existing
ID/EX, EX/MEM and MEM/WB boundaries, add one fall-through fetch slot,
and resolve a store's late data dependency at MEM instead of stalling
its independent address calculation in EX. Keep single issue and
single retirement. This is a structural change to buffering and operand
consumption, with the existing predictor and arithmetic units retained.

The fetch slot contains PC, instruction and the saved predicted_taken
bit, never operand values. Decode sees the saved slot when occupied,
otherwise the live response. Compute logical availability as
queued_valid || io_imemReady and apply the existing backend hazards to
that head. All source comparisons, decode and register reads refer to
the selected head, not the independently advancing physical fetch bus.
Do not make source-index or payload selection depend on redirect or
validity. Preserve the champion's registered one-hot forwarding masks.

With consume denoting an accepted decode head, accept a physical bus
response when io_imemReady && (!queued_valid || consume), except on
reset/recovery. Advance the request PC and its existing prediction only
on that acceptance. An empty consumed live response bypasses storage;
an empty held response fills the slot. Consuming an occupied slot either
replaces it with an accepted response or empties it. A full held slot
remains stable. Separate payload capture from validity so recovery
does not become a wide data-input mux. Recovery overrides fetch stalls,
clears the saved slot and younger ID/EX validity, and installs the exact
redirect PC. Save predictions on acceptance rather than recomputing
them on dequeue. Do not add a registered fetch latency in the empty case.

Derive actual source-use information from validated instruction decode.
Register-register ALU/M operations and conditional branches need both
sources in EX; OP-IMM, loads and JALR need rs1; stores need rs1 in EX
and rs2 in MEM; LUI, AUIPC and JAL need neither register source.
Preserve default-illegal decoding and all reserved-encoding checks.
An unused raw field must not create a load/multiply-use bubble. Keep
raw source addresses and architectural RVFI values correctly tracked;
execution-use qualification must not disable required RVFI capture.

Add an explicit late_store_data bit to the ID/EX and EX/MEM payloads.
Set it on an accepted legal store when its rs2 matches a valid,
nonzero-rd LOAD or multiply currently in EX that will become the store's
immediate older producer. Do not add a bubble for this rs2-only match.
Continue to stall if the same producer supplies the store's rs1, or if
an actual EX operand of any other instruction needs the late result.
If such a stall occurs, recompute the pending store-data classification
when decode finally advances; never save a mark for a producer whose
pipeline position has changed. Use explicit late-producer tag matching
rather than relying on raw_rs2_mask[1], since multiply is deliberately
excluded from ordinary EX/MEM forwarding eligibility.

In the store's MEM cycle, select retained wb_w_data when
late_store_data is set, otherwise the captured EX store operand.
The adjacent older load or multiply is then in MEM/WB, so its completed
value is available from a register. Apply byte/halfword replication
AFTER this selection. Capture this exact chosen value as the store's
RVFI rs2_rdata and derive RVFI mem_wdata from the same replicated data.
Keep the existing independent rs1/address calculation, memory alignment
checks, load extraction and memory-request semantics. There is no new
memory read, speculation beyond an unresolved older memory operation,
posted store retirement, or combinational dmemRData-to-EX arithmetic.

A marked store and its immediately older producer advance together
under the existing global data-memory hold. If an older load stalls,
retain the store in ID/EX and do not issue it. If the store itself
stalls in MEM after the producer retires, MEM/WB must retain its value
while clearing only valid, exactly as in the current forwarding design.
Thus late store data and byte enables remain stable until acceptance.
Never gate the retained data selection with current WB valid or w_en.
Bubble/reset the new metadata with the corresponding stage; wrong-path
stores cannot write memory. Preserve youngest-producer priority and x0.
Qualify late producers consistently with actual valid execution and
trap suppression; a misaligned load must not become an architectural
writer. For a marked store, also save a fallback source choice that
ignores the immediate late producer: use the prospective older MEM/WB
writer if its qualified nonzero tag matches rs2, otherwise the captured
register-file value. Resolve and capture that fallback in EX. In MEM,
use late wb_w_data only if the retained MEM/WB tag and trap-qualified
reg_write still identify the intended producer; otherwise use the
captured fallback. This handles a misaligned load suppressing its write
without putting address alignment on the decode/fetch hold path. The
retained producer qualification must survive valid clearing on a held
store, just like its data. Legal multiplies cannot fault but follow the
same mechanism. Test an older same-rd writer followed by a faulting
load and a marked store so stale register snapshots cannot pass.

Leave ordinary ALU, branch, multiply and division execution unchanged.
Preserve all real and ALTOPS arithmetic, nine-cycle division occupancy,
divider operand capture, stable blocked requests, exact-once channel-0
retirement, nret=1 ports and the unchanged bounded-liveness checks.
Do not compensate for a correctness failure by changing formal depths,
bus timing, benchmark sources, CRCs, wrappers or decoder legality.

The six-percent fitness estimate has low confidence. It assumes the
small buffer retains most of r10s1's measured stall-hiding benefit and
consumption-stage interlocks remove enough additional bubbles to clear
the margin. This final combination has not been implemented or timed;
its gain is a forecast. Isolated arithmetic-replication and additional
fetch-stage prototypes examined during preparation regressed and are
not part of this proposal. Main risks are a small dynamic population
of removable dependencies, new hazard-control fanout, and the late
store-data mux affecting memory-interface timing.

cycles. This is the additional cycle-saving target, not a measured
result. The fitness must exceed 182.46424 iter/sec; retain the champion
if it does not. Run unchanged formal and full RVFI cosimulation with
both bus stalls, real M-extension tests and canonical CoreMark CRC,
UART, timing-marker and memory-bound checks.

title: Register predictor recovery with separate successor targets and a recovery barrier
motivation:
Prior predictor storage changes and latency-preserving feedback retiming
left either EX recovery or the backend limiting Fmax. Direction accuracy
has limited remaining headroom: an architectural CoreMark trace has
46,342 conditional misses and 13,735 JALRs inside the markers, against
4,230,003 champion cycles. This proposal instead cuts late EX feedback
with a registered recovery event, accepting one extra cycle on a miss.
Separate target registers avoid selecting a wide recovery address with
the late forwarded branch predicate before that register boundary.

hypothesis.motivation:
Prior predictor storage changes and latency-preserving feedback retiming
left either EX recovery or the backend limiting Fmax. Direction accuracy
has limited remaining headroom: an architectural CoreMark trace has
46,342 conditional misses and 13,735 JALRs inside the markers, against

Separate target registers avoid selecting a wide recovery address with

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Keep the current 64-entry agree predictor and exact direct B/J prediction.
Register the advancing EX recovery event for use by IF and the hazard
unit in the following cycle. Capture four distinct recovery fields:
qualified mismatch valid, actual_taken, the resolved transfer target,
and PC+4. The transfer target is is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target,
without an actual_taken-controlled fallthrough mux before its register.
Select registered transfer target versus registered PC+4 using registered
actual_taken when driving IF's recovery address. These are recovery
metadata registers; keep the existing single fetch-PC register.

Register each qualified EX training event's valid, six-bit PC index and
agreement bit on the same boundary. Apply the event to the existing
per-entry saturating counters on the following edge. Clear both event
valids when no new event arrives; do not hold a valid pulse through a
stall or discard an older training event during recovery. Preserve the
current local counter update implementation, initial weak-agree state,
PC[7:2] indexing and saved predicted_taken bit.

A pending recovery must kill the extra younger instruction that reached
ID/EX before the registered event became visible. Feed EX a copy of
ID/EX with valid masked by !recovery_valid. This mask must suppress
next_reg_write, divider start, further redirects and training. Raw data
and decoded payload remain untouched. Route only registered recovery to
IF and the hazard unit; do not add an immediate EX-to-ID flush bypass.
Registered recovery overrides an instruction-bus stall, installs the
selected recovery PC, and clears younger ID/EX validity on that edge.

During this recovery cycle retain the resolving control transfer in
EX/MEM and prevent its transfer into MEM/WB: use
    ex_stall = existing_dmem_stall || recovery_valid
    mem_hold_wb = existing_hold_mem_wb || recovery_valid.
The previously older WB instruction still retires once, and mem_hold_wb
clears WB validity while retaining forwarding data. On the next edge the
control transfer advances once and EX/MEM receives the invalid younger
bubble. This is a one-cycle recovery barrier in the actual pipeline,
including link-register writeback, not an RVFI-only delay. It does not
add another cycle to fetching the corrected path. It keeps a recovered
branch followed immediately by a nine-cycle division within the existing
ten-cycle ready-bus retirement-gap limit. Without this barrier a directed
branch-to-DIV sequence produces an unacceptable eleven-cycle gap.

The recovery event can only be captured when the resolving transfer
advances past any older dmem hold. Therefore EX/MEM contains that branch
or jump during recovery, with no memory side effects; the older memory
request was already accepted. Assert this condition and verify that no
wrong-path store, load, multiply or DIV/REM launches or survives. Retain
reset priority, event cancellation on reset, all legal/illegal and
misaligned transfer semantics, JALR bit-zero clearing and link values.
RVFI reports resolved pc_next and actual operands with one retirement
and monotonic order, never predicted successors. Keep nret=1 and all
external ports, arithmetic and formal/progress bounds unchanged.

This is one predictor feedback-pipeline change. Do not combine it with
a fetch queue, new predictor policy, target cache, return stack, branch
comparator rewrite, trap-control rewrite or arithmetic optimization.
The expected benefit is lower load and shorter logic from EX resolution
to the high-fanout PC/flush/training sinks. The cost is one additional
recovery cycle per miss and more recovery metadata registers.

An isolated prototype measured Gowin placement options 0/1/2 at
74.479, 73.648 and 73.648 MHz, median 73.648 MHz, with 5,414 LUT4s,
1,288 registers and 40 LUT RAMs in option zero. The worst reported path
remained in the first divider recurrence. Canonical stalled CoreMark
completed in 4,289,458 bracketed cycles, with all five CRCs, validation
text, markers and bounds accepted by the unchanged evaluator checks.
Calculated fitness is 171.69535 iterations/second, 1.5734 percent BELOW
174.44. The minus-two-percent forecast records this observed regression;
the prototype DOES NOT qualify as a replacement. At this cycle count,
acceptance requires median Fmax above 78.26727 MHz. Retain the champion
unless the final implementation exceeds 182.46424 iterations/second.

The exact prototype passed full RVFI cosimulation for selftest and all
three random programs, each with ready buses and with both random bus
stalls: eight passing cases. Sixteen additional branch/JALR-to-DIV/REM
cases passed architectural comparison and wrong-path store suppression;
every ready-bus case retained a maximum ten-cycle retirement gap.
All 53 unchanged nret=1 ALTOPS formal checks passed in isolated staging,
including liveness, unique, register consistency and PC forwarding.
Real-M formal-deep was not run; arithmetic RTL is unchanged.
Independent delayed-event unit coverage remains an implementation gate.

Validate the delayed event protocol with an independent accepted-event
queue and the original binary counter oracle. Cover back-to-back branch
training, same-index aliases, both direction misses, JALR, reset with a
pending event, simultaneous instruction/data stalls, and younger stores
or divisions on the discarded path. Check recovery followed immediately
by each DIV/REM operation against the unchanged ten-cycle progress
assertion. Update only obsolete cycle/policy snapshots, retaining every
architectural, trap, exact-once and arithmetic assertion. Run unchanged
formal, full RVFI cosim, canonical stalled CoreMark with all five CRCs,
UART validation, bounds and markers, and median vendor timing.

title: Retain EX/MEM payload data when injecting an inert bubble
motivation:
The champion scores 174.44 iterations/sec at 73.790 MHz and 4,230,003
bracketed CoreMark cycles. Earlier r3s0/r3s1 work removed wide payload
clearing from frontend recovery, but ex_stage still clears the complete
EX/MEM bundle for invalid EX slots and every unfinished division cycle.
That drives wide ALU, multiplier-partial and store-data zeroing logic
from bubble controls. Test payload retention at this existing boundary
while explicitly suppressing every bubble's control effects.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion scores 174.44 iterations/sec at 73.790 MHz and 4,230,003
bracketed CoreMark cycles. Earlier r3s0/r3s1 work removed wide payload
clearing from frontend recovery, but ex_stage still clears the complete
EX/MEM bundle for invalid EX slots and every unfinished division cycle.
That drives wide ALU, multiplier-partial and store-data zeroing logic
from bubble controls. Test payload retention at this existing boundary
while explicitly suppressing every bubble's control effects.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only ex_stage's whole-bundle assignment in the
execute_busy || !in.valid bubble arm. Instead of reg_q <= '0, assign
reg_q.valid <= 1'b0 and reg_q.ctrl <= '0, leaving every other EX/MEM
field unassigned in that arm so it retains its preceding value. Keep
the complete ctrl_t clear, not merely valid or reg_write. This is one
local sequential-control micro-optimization; no stage, operation,
execution latency, hazard rule or memory transaction is added.

Preserve the existing priority exactly: reset clears the entire bundle;
dmem stall holds the entire bundle; div_done transfers div_metadata_q
and the division result; execute_busy or invalid EX inserts the inert
control bubble; otherwise capture the complete original normal payload.
Do not apply this transformation to reset, ID/EX, MEM/WB, divider banks
or divider metadata. Leave all normal data assignments and their
arithmetic/forwarding expressions unchanged.

In particular, retain alu_result, mul_partials, write_data, rd and RVFI
metadata through a bubble. Clearing ctrl guarantees mem_read=mem_write=
reg_write=mem_to_reg=0 and alu_op=ALU_ADD in that bubble. The retained rd
must not become a prospective producer: mem_stage.next_reg_write derives
from the cleared control, so it stays false. Valid must be zero even
though data remains nonzero. Existing memory valid/control qualification
prevents requests; WB cannot write or retire the bubble. The inactive
address/data bus and invalid RVFI payload may differ, but every accepted
request and valid retirement must remain identical.

This is distinct from capturing a new arbitrary payload on bubble edges:
the proposed payload is held, while its complete control is cleared.
Preserve MEM/WB's independent hold_wb rule, including retained forwarding
data after valid clears. Do not add current-valid gating to WB forwarding
or alter saved ID/EX operand masks. A held division continues to use its
captured request metadata, and its completed result retains the existing
priority over bubble insertion. Keep every trap, decoder default, source
priority, nret=1 port, ALTOPS formula and real arithmetic operation intact.

The intended benefit is replacing per-bit bubble zeroing on the wide EX
results with register holding, allowing native clock-enable mapping and
reducing control-dependent data muxing. The explicit control clear keeps
invalid retained data inert. Area and routing may improve, but enable
fanout and unchanged divider/branch paths can prevent any Fmax gain.
Judge mapped vendor timing, not an assumed advantage from RTL form.

An isolated prototype of exactly this change passed both existing pipeline
pytest runners, including the real arithmetic suite and the ALTOPS multiply
suite, with unchanged assertions and exact-cycle expectations. Gowin
placement options 0/1/2 measured 71.334, 73.685 and 73.685 MHz, giving a
73.685 MHz median. Area was 5,396 LUT4s and 1,214 registers, with unchanged
40 LUT RAMs, four BSRAMs and two DSPs. The worst paths still ran from
retained WB selection through EX/forwarding into fetch recovery.
At the verified unchanged CoreMark cycle count this yields 174.1961
iter/sec, approximately 0.14 percent below the champion. Therefore the
forecast is zero percent with low confidence, reflecting a near-neutral
measured result rather than a claim of an accepted improvement. Reproduce
the vendor and correctness gates during implementation; this prototype
does not justify replacing the champion at the required margin.

Full RVFI cosimulation subsequently passed selftest and three random
programs, each with and without simultaneous instruction/data stalls,
eight cases total. Canonical CoreMark passed all five required CRCs,
UART validation, memory bounds, completion and timing-bracket checks,
retaining exactly 4,230,003 bracketed cycles. Full-core standard formal
was not run for this prototype and remains an implementation gate.

Preserve every existing assertion. Add directed sequences that leave
nonzero ALU/store/multiply payloads immediately before invalid-slot and
division-busy bubbles. Check bubble valid and complete controls are zero,
payload retention, no false producer matches from retained rd, no extra
store/load acceptance and no extra writeback or retirement. Exercise
back-to-back DIV/REM, completion followed by a dependent consumer, load
and multiply interlocks, redirect squashes, reset during a held division,
and simultaneous instruction/data stalls. Check stable active memory
requests and exact RVFI source/result/memory/PC/order fields. Do not relax
any existing mask-hold, exact-cycle, trap, progress or arithmetic checks.

Run unchanged full-core standard formal and RVFI cosimulation, and retain
canonical CoreMark CRC/UART/bounds/timing-marker validation. Unit-test
success alone does not establish full formal correctness. Expect exactly
4,230,003 bracketed CoreMark cycles for the same stall sequence. Acceptance
requires fitness strictly above 182.46424 iter/sec, approximately 77.184
MHz median Gowin Fmax at that cycle count. Retain the champion unless the
greater-than-4.6-percent gain is actually measured.

title: Retimed operand capture behind a one-entry elastic fetch slot
motivation:
Structural r10s1 saved 207,170 CoreMark cycles with a one-entry fetch
buffer, but its 72.497 MHz median missed the acceptance margin. Larger
buffers and moving selection past decode did not resolve the timing cost.
The champion repeatedly exposes older WB load forwarding through EX
arithmetic and branch recovery as limiting paths. Retiming the older
bypass and PC/immediate selection into operand capture can recover the
clock margin needed to make a small elastic frontend worthwhile. This
proposal restructures the fetch/decode/execute boundary while retaining
all backend arithmetic, predictor behavior and retirement width.

hypothesis.motivation:
Structural r10s1 saved 207,170 CoreMark cycles with a one-entry fetch
buffer, but its 72.497 MHz median missed the acceptance margin. Larger
buffers and moving selection past decode did not resolve the timing cost.
The champion repeatedly exposes older WB load forwarding through EX
arithmetic and branch recovery as limiting paths. Retiming the older
bypass and PC/immediate selection into operand capture can recover the
clock margin needed to make a small elastic frontend worthwhile. This
proposal restructures the fetch/decode/execute boundary while retaining
all backend arithmetic, predictor behavior and retirement width.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Build one elastic operand-admission path: one fall-through instruction
slot ahead of decode, with completed older results and PC/immediate
selection captured before the existing ID/EX boundary. EX then selects
between a prepared operand register and the immediately older EX/MEM
result. Keep single issue, single retirement, the existing load/multiply
bubble, and nine-cycle division. Do not add an execution stage.

The fetch slot holds only PC, instruction and the saved predicted_taken
bit. Decode sees the slot when occupied, otherwise the live response.
Select payload solely from registered occupancy. Hazards and prospective
forwarding compare the selected instruction's raw source fields, never
the independently advancing physical bus response. Logical availability
is head_valid || io_imemReady. Preserve conservative raw-source interlocks;
source-use filtering and late store-data forwarding are not included.

Outside reset/recovery, with stall denoting the selected decode head's
ordinary hold condition, accept a physical response when
io_imemReady && (!head_valid || !stall). Advance the request PC and its
existing prediction only on acceptance. On an empty consumed response,
pass directly to ID/EX without storing a second copy. On an empty held
response, fill the slot. Consuming an occupied slot replaces it with an
accepted response or empties it; a full held slot remains stable.
Separate wide payload capture from validity: head_load = head_valid XOR
stall, and when head_load capture {request_pc, imem_data, prediction}.
This can sample invalid responses harmlessly. On a normal consuming edge
head_valid_next = head_valid && fetch_accept; on a held edge an accepted
response sets head_valid, otherwise retain it. Reset clears occupancy
and payload; redirect overrides the PC hold and clears slot/ID validity.
Wrong-path payload captures cannot execute. Predictions are saved on
fetch acceptance rather than recomputed when dequeued.

Expose the final pre-register MEM writeback value and valid/trap-qualified
producer tag. The value is the same load, reconstructed multiply or
normal result that WB will write after this edge. Use the ordinary selection
mem_to_reg ? load_data : is_multiply ? multiply_result : in.alu_result. Keep real and ALTOPS multiplication selection consistent.
Producer qualification is in.valid && trap_adjusted_reg_write && rd!=0;
a misaligned load must not override an older architectural writer.

For each decoded source, set capture_rs? when this MEM producer matches.
Capture raw rs?_val = capture_rs? ? mem_capture_data : rf_rs?_data.
The register file keeps its existing WB write-first behavior, so the
fallback includes an already-retiring producer. In addition capture two
prepared ALU operands independently from these same original inputs:
  alu_a_val = is_auipc ? PC : capture_rs1 ? mem_capture_data : rf_rs1_data;
  alu_b_val = alu_src ? imm : capture_rs2 ? mem_capture_data : rf_rs2_data.
Use these ordinary priority expressions; a masked one-hot capture variant
was measured and regressed, so it is not the proposed implementation.
Keep raw values
separately for branches, stores, divider launch and RVFI. Use normal
ID/EX payload enables, independent of recovery; flush validity separately.

Register the prospective match against the current EX producer, using
existing trap-qualified next_reg_write and excluding multiply as today.
For each raw EX operand, choose EX/MEM.alu_result on this younger match,
otherwise the corrected captured rs?_val. For ALU operands, enable that
same younger bypass only when the operand is not PC/immediate, otherwise
use alu_a_val/alu_b_val. Each EX data selection is a two-input mux.
Remove the MEM/WB data source from all EX raw and ALU operand muxes.
The youngest producer retains priority even when both older stages write
the same register. Do not bypass a load address or multiply partials:
the unchanged late-result interlock ensures the next advancing consumer
captures the completed MEM result instead. x0 remains hardwired zero.

A real data-memory hold freezes the consumer operand registers and masks
together, with EX/MEM also held. Unready load data must never be captured
as an accepted consumer. Keep MEM/WB retained-data behavior; no removal
of its hold logic is required. Division captures fully resolved operands
once and retains them while older stages drain. Its completion and the
following consumer keep the existing forwarding/advancement schedule.
Invalid stale producer payloads must not qualify for the new capture
bypass. Preserve misalignment suppression and the fallback value when a
would-be writer traps. Keep raw RVFI source values even for fields that
are not architectural execution operands.

Keep nret=1 and every external port unchanged. Preserve decoder legality,
all real/ALTOPS arithmetic, memory request semantics, exact-once ordered
retirement, reset cancellation, wrong-path suppression and the unchanged
formal liveness bound. Predictor, divider internals, multiplier latency,
register-file write timing and memory architecture remain unchanged.
This is a structural timing/buffering hypothesis; RVFI-only work cannot
supply the proposed fitness improvement.

A prototype of this one-slot architecture passed eight full-RVFI
architectural cosims: selftest and three random programs, each with and
without both bus stalls. Canonical stalled CoreMark took 4,022,833
bracketed cycles, with all CRCs, validation text and bounds checks passing.
Gowin placement options 0/1/2 measured 70.826/73.307/73.307 MHz, median
73.307 MHz and 182.22730 iter/sec: 4.464 percent above 174.44, narrowly
below the required 4.6 percent. This is an improvement hypothesis, but
the measured prototype is not yet a qualifying champion replacement.
Full formal qualification of this exact one-slot version remains required;
a two-slot relative passed all 53 unchanged checks, which is not a proof
of this version. All arithmetic RTL and real/ALTOPS formulas are unchanged.

Measure median Gowin Fmax over all three placement options times measured
iterations/cycle. At 4,022,833 cycles, acceptance needs more than
73.402317 MHz and 182.46424 iter/sec. The four-percent estimate rounds the
measured preliminary gain and has low confidence because it does not
clear the acceptance margin. Do not claim acceptance without remeasurement. Main risks are
MEM result-to-ID capture delay, decode/head selection fanout, and the
unchanged first divider recurrence becoming the frequency limit.
Run the unchanged complete formal suite, real arithmetic tests and full
architectural cosim. Add directed tests of every fetch-slot transition,
saved predictions, reset/recovery while full, older WB and MEM writers,
younger same-rd priority, late results, trap-suppressed producers and
held operands. Preserve architectural checks when adapting internal
forwarding-shape and fetch-scheduling assertions.

title: Normalize prediction checking to shared equality and ordering predicates
motivation:
The champion's reported worst path runs from registered forwarding
selection through EX to the fetch PC. Prior predictor experiments
show that accuracy alone offers little headroom, while replicated
source-pair comparisons (r10s2) and an explicit two-bit comparison
tree (r9s0) did not improve whole-core timing. A smaller, shared
branch-outcome checker can reduce logic and routing at both recovery
and agree-training sinks without changing prediction accuracy or
recovery latency. This proposal keeps native comparison operators
and factors the six branch conditions around two shared predicates.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion's reported worst path runs from registered forwarding
selection through EX to the fetch PC. Prior predictor experiments
show that accuracy alone offers little headroom, while replicated
source-pair comparisons (r10s2) and an explicit two-bit comparison
tree (r9s0) did not improve whole-core timing. A smaller, shared
branch-outcome checker can reduce logic and routing at both recovery
and agree-training sinks without changing prediction accuracy or
recovery latency. This proposal keeps native comparison operators
and factors the six branch conditions around two shared predicates.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace only the branch-condition case statement in ex_stage.sv with
one equality comparison and one unsigned ordering comparison of the
existing fully forwarded rs1 and rs2. Let op = in.ctrl.branch_op:
    equal = (rs1 == rs2)
    unsigned_less = (rs1 < rs2)
    less = (!op[1] && (rs1[31] ^ rs2[31]))
           ? rs1[31] : unsigned_less
    branch_cond = (op[2] || !op[1])
                  && ((op[2] ? less : equal) ^ op[0]).

op[2] selects equality versus ordering; op[0] selects the complementary
condition. For signed BLT/BGE, opposite operand signs determine less
directly; equal signs use the same unsigned comparison as BLTU/BGEU.
The explicit validity factor forces reserved branch_op 2 and 3 false.
Preserve decoder validation independently: this factor must not make
any reserved encoding legal. Use ordinary 32-bit unsigned logic for
rs1 and rs2 and retain their exact existing forwarding selection.

Feed this predicate into the existing branch_taken, actual_taken,
redirect and train_agree equations without changing qualification or
timing. Keep all six legal comparisons exact, including signed extrema,
equal operands and unsigned high-bit cases. Preserve the current
target adders, alignment traps, JAL/JALR handling, architectural pc_next,
direction metadata, 64-entry binary agree table, direct prediction,
same-cycle recovery, and local counter updates. This is a single
predictor-resolution change; there is no new stage, training delay,
target cache, forwarding replication or arithmetic-unit redesign.

Preserve raw source-index paths and validity-only squashes. The
checker must still see retained MEM/WB forwarding values during dmem
holds, respect younger-writer priority and x0, and resolve only when
EX advances. Do not gate operand data with current WB validity.
Keep nret=1, exact-once retirement and side effects, all RVFI fields,
the original ten-cycle ready-bus progress bound, decoder legality,
memory handshakes, real M-extension and ALTOPS behavior unchanged.

The intended benefit is less duplicated outcome logic and simpler
complementary-condition selection before predictor recovery and
training. The cost is a shared comparison cone whose fanout can
worsen placement; an unchanged divider or forwarded ALU can remain
the clock limit. This is not an accuracy or IPC improvement.

An isolated prototype of these exact equations measured Gowin
placement options 0/1/2 at 69.896, 73.461 and 73.461 MHz, median
73.461 MHz. Option zero used 5,342 LUT4s and 1,214 registers,
saving 80 LUT4s against the champion, with unchanged 40 LUT RAMs,
four BSRAMs and two DSPs. Its worst reported path was in the first
divider recurrence. Canonical CoreMark with both random bus stalls
retained 4,230,003 marker-bracketed cycles and passed all five CRCs,
UART validation, completion and memory-bound checks.

Measured fitness is 173.66654 iterations/second, 0.4434 percent below
174.44. The minus-one-percent estimate conservatively records this
observed limitation; the prototype DOES NOT qualify as a replacement.
Retain the champion unless the final implementation exceeds
182.46424 iterations/second. At unchanged cycles that requires more
than 77.18243 MHz median Fmax. Do not combine backend optimizations
or relax verification to rescue this predictor slot.

Validation of the isolated prototype passed a combinational SAT
equivalence proof for every operand pair and all eight branch_op
encodings, all 53 unchanged nret=1 ALTOPS formal checks, the existing
pipeline and multiply-ALTOPS test runners, and eight full-RVFI cosim
cases: selftest plus three random programs, each with ready buses
and with both bus stalls. Real-arithmetic formal-deep was not run;
no arithmetic execution unit changes are proposed.

Preserve the existing independent predictor, operand, retirement
and exact-cycle oracles. Add directed architectural branch cases
covering all six legal comparisons, equal values, opposite signs,
signed extrema, unsigned values around 0x80000000, and differing
bits across the word. Exercise register, EX/MEM and retained MEM/WB
sources, load/multiply dependencies, division completion, target
misalignment and simultaneous stalls. Reproduce unchanged formal,
full RVFI cosim, canonical CoreMark validation and median vendor
timing on the final implementation before evaluating acceptance.
